title: Entergy Louisiana launches major grid resilience project in Jefferson Parish
summary: Entergy Louisiana, joined by local elected officials and community leaders, celebrated the launch of a major grid resilience project in Jefferson Parish with a ceremonial ribbon cutting…
body_text: JEFFERSON PARISH, La. – Entergy Louisiana, joined by local elected officials and community leaders, celebrated the launch of a major grid resilience project in Jefferson Parish with a ceremonial ribbon cutting, marking the beginning of a $270 million investment to strengthen the parish’s electric infrastructure and enhance reliability for customers. The project includes replacing or hardening more than 500 utility poles and other electrical infrastructure along Veterans Boulevard between the Orleans Parish line and Clearview Parkway. The project, now underway, is expected to conclude by October, weather and other working conditions permitting. The new poles are engineered to withstand wind speeds of up to 140 mph, improving the resilience of the local grid during severe weather and help reduce duration of outages. “Today’s ribbon cutting represents more than the start of a construction project. It reflects our long-term commitment to building a stronger, more resilient grid for the communities we serve,” said Phillip May, president & CEO of Entergy Louisiana . “These investments will help reduce storm impacts, improve reliability for our customers and support Jefferson Parish’s continued economic growth for decades to come.” This project is part of Entergy Louisiana’s comprehensive grid resilience plan , designed to strengthen critical infrastructure across the state and help communities better withstand the impacts of increasingly severe weather. As part of Jefferson Parish’s overall resilience program, Entergy Louisiana will upgrade hundreds of miles of infrastructure, including replacing or reinforcing approximately 8,400 distribution and transmission poles with stronger structures engineered to withstand wind speeds of up to 140 mph. Investments like this will help improve reliability for residents while supporting many of Jefferson Parish’s key industries, including environmental and engineering services, health innovation, supply chain infrastructure, and technology and design. A stronger power grid reduces costly outages, improves business continuity, strengthens supply chains and creates an environment that encourages continued economic investment and job growth. Modernized infrastructure also supports the integration of advanced technologies and renewable energy resources while helping protect communities against future extreme weather events. This resilience program was developed using a comprehensive, data-driven planning process that analyzed thousands of storm scenarios to identify projects expected to provide the greatest reliability and resilience benefits for customers. In addition to strengthening the electric system, this statewide resilience plan is expected to deliver significant long-term value. Over time, the program is projected to avoid approximately $175 million in future storm restoration costs while reducing restoration times following severe weather. It is also expected to generate an estimated $5 billion in long-term capital maintenance and investment benefits over the next 50 years through fewer emergency repairs, reduced equipment failures and longer-lasting infrastructure. Construction activities in Jefferson Parish will continue over the coming months as crews work to strengthen the local electric system safely and efficiently. Crews will be working in phases along Veterans Boulevard throughout the project. Traffic impacts are possible in certain areas while work is underway, and some planned outages may be required to safely complete portions of the project. If so, customers will receive advance notifications. About Entergy Louisiana Entergy Louisiana provides electricity to more than 1.1 million customers in 58 parishes. Entergy Louisiana is a subsidiary of Entergy Corporation (NYSE: ETR). Entergy generates, transmits and distributes electricity to power life for 3 million customers through our operating companies in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas. We’re focused on keeping costs for our customers as low as possible while providing reliable energy that our communities count on. We’re also investing in growth for the future with a more resilient, cleaner energy system that includes modern natural gas, nuclear and renewable energy generation. As a nationally recognized leader in sustainability and corporate citizenship, Entergy delivers more than $100 million in economic benefits each year to the communities we serve through philanthropy, volunteerism and advocacy. Entergy is a Fortune 500 company headquartered in New Orleans, Louisiana, and has approximately 12,000 employees. Learn more at EntergyLouisiana.com and connect with @EntergyLA on social media. Media inquiries: Brandon Scardigli [email protected] Media line: 504-576-4132

title: Answer Engine Optimization (AEO): What It Is and How It Relates to SEO and GEO
summary: Answer engine optimization (AEO) means becoming the source AI answers cite. How AEO relates to SEO and GEO, and where ecommerce teams should start.
body_text: Answer engine optimization, or AEO, is the practice of making your content the source an AI system cites when it answers a question. Instead of competing for a position in a list of links, you are competing to be the information an answer gets built from. The label is new. Most of the work is not. Google's own guidance on AI features states that "optimizing for generative AI search is optimizing for the search experience, and thus still SEO." That is worth knowing before anyone sells you a separate AEO strategy. What has genuinely changed is what gets evaluated. Answer engines describe, compare, and recommend products using whatever product information they can find and trust. For retailers, brands, and distributors that puts your product data, not just your marketing copy, in front of the thing making the recommendation. What is answer engine optimization, and how is it different from SEO? Answer engine optimization is the work of making your content easy for an AI system to reach, understand, and quote with attribution. In practice that means three things: the system can access your content, the information is complete and accurate enough to be worth repeating, and it is organized so a specific question maps to a specific answer. The honest answer on how it differs from SEO is: less than the term implies. Google's AI optimization guide is explicit that structured data "isn't required for generative AI search, and there's no special schema.org markup you need to add," though it recommends continuing to use it as part of overall SEO. The same guide says you do not need chunking, an llms.txt file, or content rewritten specifically for AI systems. One caveat matters. That guidance speaks for Google Search and its own surfaces. ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Amazon's shopping assistant retrieve differently, and none of them publishes a specification you can optimize against. That absence is exactly why the fundamentals carry the weight. So the three terms are best read as three emphases on the same work, not three disciplines. SEO GEO AEO What the label emphasizes Being found among ranked results Being represented in generated output Being credited as the source for a specific answer Where attention goes Rankings and clicks Whether your brand appears at all Whether you are cited, and for which questions Typical measurement Position, impressions, organic traffic Share of mentions across a set of prompts How often you are cited, by question What the underlying work is Content a machine can reach, trust, and match to a question The same content work as SEO The same content work as SEO The labels differ in what they measure, not in what you do. So if someone pitches AEO as separate from your SEO work, ask what the actual tasks are. If the answer is content quality, crawler access and accurate product data, that is SEO with a new name. What counts as an answer engine? An answer engine is any system that responds to a question with a synthesized answer rather than a list of sources. The ones your shoppers actually use are ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode, Microsoft Copilot, and Amazon's Alexa for Shopping, which was called Rufus until May 2026. So yes, ChatGPT is an answer engine. It is also routinely called a generative engine. The same system takes a different label depending on which acronym someone is selling, which is a good illustration of why the distinctions are thinner than they look. What does vary is how these systems find information. Some retrieve live from a search index, some rely on their own crawl, some blend both with what they already learned in training. You cannot optimize for each one separately, which is the practical argument for getting the underlying information right. How do answer engines choose what to cite? Three things have to be true before your content can appear in an answer. Each one is a gate, and failing any of them makes the others irrelevant. Can the system reach your content? If your content sits behind JavaScript that a crawler does not execute, or your robots rules block AI user agents, nothing else matters. This is the prerequisite, and it is the one teams most often skip. We cover how to check it in our guide to whether LLMs can crawl your site . Does your content answer the question as it was asked? Answer engines match a question to a passage, not to a page. Content organized around real questions with direct answers underneath them gets picked up more readily than the same information spread through narrative prose. That favors specificity. "Water resistant to 50m" can be matched to a question. "Built to handle whatever your day throws at it" cannot. Is the information trustworthy enough to repeat? A system will only attach your name to a claim it has some reason to believe. Product attributes that are consistent across your own channels, specifications that do not contradict each other between your site and your marketplace listings, and independent sources saying the same thing all make a claim safer to repeat. This is where most catalogs fail, and it is a data problem rather than a writing one. Where should ecommerce teams start with AEO? Start with the product data, because it is the raw material every answer engine works from. A catalog with missing attributes, inconsistent specification formats, and thin descriptions cannot be cited accurately, because there is nothing specific enough to cite. That means filling in missing attributes across the catalog, standardizing how values are expressed so a field means the same thing on every SKU, and making sure product pages carry the specifics shoppers actually ask about. This is ordinary product data work, and for most ecommerce teams it is the highest-leverage AEO work available. From there, three narrower paths matter, and we have dedicated guides for each: Product pages and generative search. How to structure product content so generative engines can use it: read our guide to GEO for ecommerce . Technical access. Whether AI crawlers can reach your site at all: see whether LLMs can crawl your site . Measurement. How teams track whether they show up in AI answers: see our roundup of AI visibility tools . Sequence matters. Monitoring tells you where you stand, but it will not fix a catalog that has nothing worth citing. Frequently asked questions Will AEO replace SEO? No. Google's position is that optimizing for generative AI search is still SEO, and answer engines lean heavily on search indexes to find candidate sources. What changes is measurement, not method: rankings and clicks stop describing your full visibility once answers are being read instead of links being clicked. Are AEO, GEO and AI search optimization the same thing? Close enough that the distinction rarely changes what you do. Answer engine optimization, generative engine optimization, AI search optimization, LLM SEO and AI visibility optimization all describe making your content usable by AI systems. They differ mainly in what they emphasize measuring. Pick one label internally and spend the argument budget elsewhere. What is the best answer engine optimization tool? It depends which problem you have. Monitoring tools tell you how often you appear in AI answers and for which prompts, which is useful for measurement but changes nothing about your content. Product content and PIM platforms address the data quality that determines whether you are worth citing at all. We compare the monitoring options in our roundup of AI visibility tools . How do you measure AEO? Most teams define a set of questions their buyers actually ask, then check across the major answer engines how often they are mentioned and cited for those questions. Answers vary between runs and between users, so single checks are unreliable and the signal only emerges over repeated sampling. Search Console will not show this, because a citation inside a chat interface is not a search impression. Conclusion AEO rewards what good ecommerce operations have always rewarded: product information that is complete, consistent, and specific enough to be useful. The difference is that a machine is now reading it, and it will skip what it cannot verify. That makes this a product data problem before it is a content marketing one. Hypotenuse AI helps ecommerce teams get there by filling in missing attributes and standardizing values across the catalog through product data enrichment , inside an AI-native PIM built for catalogs at enterprise scale. If your catalog is not ready to be cited, that is where to start.

title: Western Alliance Bank’s Melanie Krinsky Named 2026 Entertainment Business Visionary for Advancing Film, TV and Music Financing
summary: Melanie Krinsky, Senior Managing Director and Head of Entertainment & Media Group, has been named a 2026 Entertainment Business Visionary, recognizing her role in expanding access to film, television and music financing across North America.
body_text: PHOENIX — Western Alliance Bank (NYSE:WAL) today announced that Melanie Krinsky , Senior Managing Director and Head of its Entertainment & Media Group, has been named a 2026 Entertainment Business Visionary by the LA Times Studios, recognizing her role in expanding access to film, television and music financing across North America. Since founding the Los Angeles-based group in 2021, Krinsky has led more than $2.5 billion in financing for production, post-production, distribution and music clients. The group expanded into music industry financing in 2025, reflecting growing demand for capital across the broader entertainment ecosystem. Krinsky’s recognition reflects the growing importance of specialized financing in bringing film, television and music projects to market. Her work supports independent studios, distributors and music companies seeking flexible capital to fund production, acquisition and distribution. “Melanie has redefined how entertainment and media businesses access capital,” said Tim Bruckner, Chief Banking Officer, Regional Banking, Western Alliance Bank. “Her work is enabling clients to move projects forward in a market that continues to grow more complex.” Recent financing supported award-winning films including “Anora,” the Academy Award® Best Picture 2025 winner distributed in North America by Western Alliance client Neon, and “Everything Everywhere All at Once,” the Academy Award® Best Picture 2023 winner produced and distributed by Western Alliance client A24. Over a 40-year career, Krinsky has advised clients across film, television and music while mentoring industry professionals and advocating for greater representation across the creative economy. She is a frequent speaker on entertainment and finance panels in the U.S. and internationally. Read Krinsky’s Entertainment Business Visionary profile View the complete list of 2026 Entertainment Visionaries About Us Western Alliance Bank Western Alliance Bancorporation (NYSE: WAL) is one of the country’s top-performing banking companies and has ranked as a top U.S. bank by American Banker and Bank Director since 2016. Its primary subsidiary, Western Alliance Bank, is a leading national bank for business that puts customers first, delivering tailored business banking solutions and consumer products backed by outstanding, personalized service and specific expertise in more than 30 industries and sectors. With more than $90 billion in assets and offices nationwide, Western Alliance excels at helping businesses of all sizes capitalize on their opportunities to solve today and succeed tomorrow.

title: AWS WAF now supports a Salt Security managed rule group for API and MCP threat detection
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with AWS WAF now supports a Salt Security managed rule group for API and MCP threat detection
body_text: AWS WAF now supports the Salt Security managed rule group, available through AWS Marketplace: Salt Managed Rules for AWS WAF - AI Agent & API Security . This rule group gives AWS WAF customers detection and mitigation for API-focused attacks and for traffic from AI agents and Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoints, without writing or maintaining custom rules. The rule group detects common and complex API attack vectors, including credential brute force, excessive GraphQL queries, server-side request forgery (SSRF), prototype pollution, and JSON Web Token (JWT) anomalies. It identifies and labels traffic from Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoints, blocks unauthenticated MCP access, and adds observability into MCP interactions in AWS WAF. The rule group also applies rate limiting to sensitive request parameters, such as user identifiers and email addresses, to help mitigate enumeration and abuse. To support detection and downstream analysis, it labels request attributes including authorization headers, user identifiers, and GraphQL queries. You can subscribe to the rule group and add it to a web ACL directly in the AWS WAF console through AWS Marketplace, with no additional configuration. The rule group supports versioning, and pricing is set by Salt Security through AWS Marketplace. For a full list of supported Regions, visit the AWS Regional Services page. To get started, visit the AWS WAF console or find the Salt Security rule group in AWS Marketplace. For more information, see the AWS WAF Developer Guide .

title: The Medical Gap on Your Resume: What to Say (and What You Never Have to)
summary: Your resume owes honest dates, not a diagnosis. How to handle a medical or health gap: say nothing, add a neutral "career break" label, or one brief line.
body_text: Do you have to explain a medical gap on your resume? No. Your resume owes an employer honest dates and a truthful work history, not the reason you were away. You can leave the gap unexplained, add a neutral line like "Career Break, 2023–2024," or write one short, non-medical sentence noting the leave is resolved and you're available. Naming the illness is a personal choice, never a requirement. In the US an employer generally can't even ask about a medical condition before making a job offer. Pick the lightest option that lets a reader move on. There's a particular kind of dread that comes with updating a resume after a health crisis. You're staring at a blank stretch between two jobs, and the timeline feels like it's about to narrate the worst year of your life to a stranger. It isn't. A gap is a fact on a page. It is not a confession, and you are not on the stand. This piece is about the resume specifically. It's the one document where you have the most control and owe the least explanation. The one honest sentence some people add to a cover letter is a separate call, and the "so, what happened here?" conversation lives in the interview, which we'll get to. First, the page itself. What goes on it, what stays off it, and how to lay it out so a reader sees your work before they count the months. The short version: your resume owes dates, not a diagnosis Two things belong on a resume and are non-negotiable: your employment dates have to be accurate, and the work history you list has to be true. That's the whole contract. Nothing in it requires a reason for time off. People tie themselves in knots here because the gap feels like a question the resume is asking on the employer's behalf. It isn't, really. A recruiter scanning your history wants to account for the time, confirm you can do the job, and see that you're available now. The specific cause of a break rarely factors into any of that. A blank between two dated roles reads as ordinary far more often than people fear, because most careers have one by now. If it helps to think about the deeper question of whether a gap hurts you at all, we wrote a whole recruiter's-eye piece on whether employers actually care about career gaps . Short answer, the gap is rarely the thing that sinks a candidacy. This post assumes the gap is already there, and you just need to know what to type into that space. Three ways to handle it, side by side There are really only three moves, and all three are honest. The trick is matching the move to your situation instead of reaching for the one that feels safest in the moment. Say nothing. Let the dates stand and let the gap be blank. This works when the break is short, or old, or already accounted for by everything around it. A four-month space from early 2024 does not need a caption. Adding one often does more harm than the silence would have. Label it, neutrally. Drop a plain entry into your timeline where a job would go: Career Break, 2023–2024 . That's it. No reason, no story. A neutral label with dates tells a reader the time is accounted for and there's nothing to chase, which is usually all they wanted to know. "Personal Leave" and "Family and Health Leave" do the same job if the wording sits better with you. Add one honest, non-medical line. When the break is long and recent enough that a reader will wonder, a single forward-looking sentence can settle the question before it's asked: Took a planned medical leave; fully resolved and available for full-time work. Notice what that line does and doesn't do. It's accurate, and it looks forward, toward the job rather than the past. What it never does is name a condition. It helps to picture how these look in the actual block of your work history. Option one is two roles stacked with a visible space between the end date of one and the start of the next, and a reader's eye slides over it faster than you'd think. Option two puts a line where a job title would go, something like "Career Break, 2023–2024," sitting in the same left-aligned column as your positions so it reads as a deliberate entry instead of a missing one. Option three is that same entry with a short clause hanging off it. None of the three changes the architecture of the resume. They only change how much the blank space is allowed to say. Most people land on option one or two. Option three earns its place only in the narrow cases we'll get to below. What you never have to put on a resume Here's the part worth reading twice. You are never obligated to put your diagnosis, your prognosis, your treatment, or the reason for your leave on a resume. Not the word, and not even a hint of it. Whether to disclose a health condition is your decision and yours alone, and choosing privacy is not the same as hiding something. The general legal backdrop supports that instinct, and this is a good moment for a clear caveat: what follows is general information, not legal advice, and your own situation deserves a professional who knows the specifics. With that said, in the US the Americans with Disabilities Act generally prohibits an employer from asking disability-related questions or requiring a medical exam before it makes you a conditional job offer. An employer can ask if you're able to do the job and how you'd approach it. It generally cannot ask what's wrong with you. The ADA's employment rules generally reach employers with 15 or more staff. When a form or a screen can't ask the question, a resume certainly doesn't have to answer it. So the "why" is optional in the strongest sense. Some people share a sliver of it for their own comfort. Many share nothing. Both are completely normal, and neither is a strategic mistake. Vague, but honest: the line that actually works If you do decide to write something, aim for a phrase that's neutral, true, and pointed forward. Those three qualities are what separate a line that reassures from a line that raises eyebrows. Neutral means the line names a category and nothing more. "Health matter," "medical leave," "personal leave," any of those. Keep it accurate too, since the dates around it are checkable and you never want the wording fighting the facts. Then let the sentence land on the job ahead instead of the time behind you. A working template: [Neutral reason]; now resolved and available. Fill it in and you get lines like Full-time medical leave, 2023–2024; resolved and ready for full-time work , or the even shorter Career Break for a health matter (resolved) . Both say enough without saying too much. What you're avoiding is the apology and the backstory. No "unfortunately," no "had to step away due to a serious," no reassurances about how it won't happen again. A person who's fine doesn't over-explain, and the tone of the line does as much work as the words. Calm and short reads as calm and short. Never invent a job, never move a date There's a tempting shortcut that turns a small problem into a large one: filling the gap with a job that didn't happen, or nudging your real dates to make the space disappear. Skip both. Omitting a reason isn't lying. Inventing a role that never existed is a different thing entirely, and the distinction matters, because employment history is one of the most routinely checked facts in hiring. Background screens and employment verifications exist specifically to confirm titles and dates, and payroll-fed databases like The Work Number can surface the actual months you clocked in somewhere. A fabricated job or a doctored date doesn't read as a rounding error when it's found. It reads as a reason not to trust anything else on the page, and it usually ends the process on the spot. We broke down exactly what these checks do and don't surface in this guide to what a background check actually shows . The honest version costs you nothing you'd actually want to keep. A true blank on your timeline is defensible forever, while a clever fiction becomes a small landmine you carry into every future conversation about the role. How much is enough Almost always: a label, one line, or nothing. That's the whole range. The instinct to over-explain is human, and it backfires anyway. Picture a recruiter with forty resumes to clear before lunch. On yours they hit three careful sentences about a health condition sitting where a job should be, and the first thing that fires isn't sympathy, it's "why did this need three sentences." The detail you offered as reassurance reads as a flag instead. Space is the tell: the more room the gap takes up on the page, the more important it starts to look. One tidy line, or a clean blank, says the opposite. This is handled, now let's talk about the work. Think of the gap as a footnote, not a headline. Here's a test that works: read your own resume top to bottom at the pace a recruiter actually reads, the quick skim of a few seconds, and notice where your attention lands. If it snags on the empty stretch instead of your most recent title, the layout is pointing at the wrong thing, and the fix is to make the recent work louder rather than the gap quieter. Where the gap sits on the page Layout does quiet work here. You can play a gap down without hiding it, and the difference between those two things is the whole game. Keep an honest reverse-chronological order. That's still what most recruiters and applicant tracking systems expect, and trying to dodge it usually costs you more than the gap does. Lead the page with a strong summary and your most recent relevant work, so a reader meets your skills before they start counting months. If you're coming back into a slightly different lane, leaning on transferable skills up top puts the focus where you want it. The format to steer clear of is the pure "functional" or skills-only layout that drops dates entirely. Recruiters read those as a sign you're hiding something, and the software behind the first screen tends to parse them badly. One more small lever: year-only dates. Listing "2023" and "2024" instead of the exact months can quietly shrink a seven-month gap into nothing, and that's not dishonest, since you're just being less granular. It has a limit, though. Year-only dates won't hide a long gap, and a reader who sees "2019" next to "2021" may fill the blank year with their own worst guess, so treat it as a way to soften a short gap, not a cloak for a big one. If your timeline feels cluttered by the whole thing, it's often easier to rebuild it cleanly in a resume builder than to keep nudging a document that's fighting you. For the general mechanics of dates and formatting around any gap, this career-gap resume walkthrough covers the nuts and bolts. Not sure how loud your gap looks? Get a free, second-pair-of-eyes review of your resume and see exactly how a recruiter reads your timeline. Review my resume → When a line of context helps, and when silence is fine The one-line option isn't a default. It's a tool for a specific shape of gap, and using it in the wrong place just draws a circle around something a reader would've skated past. A line earns its place when the gap is long, recent, and obvious enough that a reader will stop and wonder no matter what you do. A two-year blank ending last month is going to raise the question in someone's head. A neutral label there gets ahead of it and reads as steady rather than evasive. The same logic covers a caregiving break, which is common enough now that a plain Family Caregiving, 2022–2024 reads as completely unremarkable. If that's closer to your situation, the caregiver resume guide goes deeper on framing the skills that period built. Silence wins the rest of the time. Short gaps, gaps from years ago, gaps that later dates already explain. Adding a caption to a quiet, old, three-month break is like footnoting a sentence nobody questioned. When in doubt about a small gap, leave it. The blank is doing less damage than the explanation would. If the reason is mental health Every rule above holds, without an asterisk. A break for depression, anxiety, burnout, or a hospitalization is a health matter, and a resume treats it exactly like any other. You owe no detail. A neutral label is the standard move, and "Career Break" or "Health Leave" covers it fully. One honest observation, offered as a choice and not a rule: a lot of people reach for the plain word "health" rather than "mental health," and that's usually because the stigma still runs heavier for the second phrase than it should. Making that call for your own protection is completely legitimate, and so is being more open if that's who you are and the field welcomes it. There's no correct answer here, only the one you can defend without your stomach dropping. What a recruiter is actually reading for, in every version of this, is one plain thing: do you seem steady and ready to do the work. The diagnosis was never the thing being evaluated. The reassurance that does the real work: you're back now Here's the reframe that takes the pressure off the gap entirely. The quiet question behind a recruiter's eyes is less "what happened to them" and much more "are they back, and can they be counted on now." Answer that second one well, and the first mostly dissolves on its own. You answer it by looking current. Maybe that's a Google Data Analytics certificate you finished in the spring, or two months of contract work you took on to knock the rust off, or a volunteer project that leaned on the exact skills a job posting lists. Any one of those settles a reader more than a paragraph about the past ever could, because it's evidence instead of a promise. A gap that ends in "and here's what I've been sharpening lately" stops looking like a hole and starts to read like a runway. On the page, that usually lives in a short "Recent Professional Development" block sitting near the top, above or beside your work history, so it's among the first things a skimming eye lands on. You don't need a stack of entries there. One recent, dated, relevant item pulls most of the weight, because it drags attention into the present tense, which is exactly where you want the whole conversation to sit. That's the whole psychology of a return. Nobody on a hiring panel is grading your recovery; they're checking whether the person in front of them can do the role in front of them, and "resolved and current" answers that more convincingly than a backstory ever could. The interview is a different room Keep the two jobs separate. The resume's only task is to get you into the room. Whatever brief context you choose to share out loud belongs in the conversation, not on the page, and it can stay just as light there. If the gap comes up in an interview, one calm sentence handles it: I took some time out for a health matter, it's fully resolved, and I'm glad to be back. Then pivot to the work. You still don't owe a diagnosis in that room either. You control how much you share, and "resolved, and here's why I'm a fit" is a complete answer. We put together a fuller script for that exact moment in our guide to explaining career gaps during an interview , and if you're deciding whether to add a sentence to your application letter, the cover-letter gap post covers that call. If you want the wider map of how a recruiter moves a candidate from resume to offer, our pillar on how hiring actually works lays out where each stage weighs what. A word if you're still in the thick of it If you're reading this mid-treatment, or in the shaky early weeks of a return, the resume is not the emergency it feels like tonight. It's a fixable document. You can label a gap in ten minutes once the fear stops running the edit, and none of the choices above are permanent. You also don't have to do it alone. There are genuinely free, no-strings resources built for exactly this: Cancer and Careers runs a free resume-review service for people with a cancer diagnosis, and places like Memorial Sloan Kettering and the National Coalition for Cancer Survivorship keep return-to-work guidance that's practical rather than preachy. Career counselors and, in some cases, an oncology social worker can help you rehearse the interview line until it stops catching in your throat. Use them. The gap on your resume is going to look enormous to you and ordinary to almost everyone reading it. That mismatch is the whole thing. Give a reader an accurate timeline, a calm label if you want one, and clear evidence that you're ready now, and you've done everything the page is actually asking of you. Frequently Asked Questions Do I legally have to disclose a medical condition on my resume? Nothing requires it. A caveat before anything else, though: this is general information, not legal advice. With that said, in the US an employer usually can't even ask about a specific medical condition until it has made you a conditional offer, and a resume comes long before that point, so it certainly doesn't have to volunteer one. Sharing is your call. If your circumstances are thorny, an employment lawyer who knows your state is the right person to ask. What's the safest way to label a health gap? A neutral entry with dates, sitting in your timeline right where a job would go: "Career Break, 2023–2024." That's the whole thing. "Personal Leave" and "Health Leave" do the same work if either reads better to you. A label like this accounts for the months, and accounting for the months is the one thing most readers are checking for. Should I just leave the gap blank instead? Often that's the better move. A break that's short, or years old, or already boxed in by the dates around it needs no caption at all. Over-explaining costs you more than the silence does. Save a written line for the gaps that are long, recent, and big enough to make someone pause on their own. Can I write "medical leave" without naming the illness? Yes, and that's exactly the move. "Medical leave" or "health matter" points at a category rather than a condition, and adding "resolved and available" turns the sentence toward the future. The diagnosis, the prognosis, the course of treatment: none of it is owed to anyone reading a resume. A category plus a forward turn is genuinely enough. Is it okay to use year-only dates to shrink the gap? For a short gap, sure. Writing "2023" and "2024" instead of the exact months isn't a lie, and it can make a five-month break more or less disappear. There's a ceiling on the trick. It won't paper over a long absence, and a reader who clocks a whole year missing between two entries may imagine something worse than what really happened. Soften a small gap with it, don't disguise a big one. What if the gap is because of my mental health? Treat it like any other health matter, because that is what it is. A neutral "Career Break" line covers it and you owe no further detail. Plenty of people go with the plain word "health" over "mental health," usually because the stigma still lands harder on the second phrase, and that's a fair personal decision rather than a rule. A recruiter is reading for readiness, not a diagnosis. Won't a background check expose my gap anyway? It can confirm your titles and your dates, which is precisely why you keep both honest and never invent a job to plug the hole. A true gap, even an unexplained one, holds up under any scrutiny. What gets people caught is the fabricated role or the shifted date. Our background-check guide walks through what actually surfaces. How do I explain the gap if they ask in the interview? Keep it to one calm sentence: "I stepped away for a health matter, it's resolved, and I'm glad to be back." Then turn the conversation toward the role. No diagnosis is owed in that room either. Our interview-gap guide has a fuller script if you want to rehearse it. Does a health gap actually hurt my chances? Far less than the 3am version of your brain insists. What raises eyebrows is an unexplained gap sitting next to skills that have gone stale, not a labeled break that ends in something recent and relevant. The gap on its own is rarely the dealbreaker. We got into the recruiter's actual read in do employers care about career gaps . I've been out for years. Is a one-line label really enough? For the resume, yes. The thing that carries a multi-year return isn't the label, it's the proof that you're current now: a certificate finished last quarter, a bit of contract work, a course, volunteering that flexed the target skills. Put a neutral label together with one recent signal like that, and the length of the break quietly stops being the headline. title: Mitutoyo MeasurLink SPC Software — MSC Industrial Supply Co.
summary: MeasurLink 11 helps metalworking shops collect inspection data faster — with easier setup, OCR-based inspection planning, and push-button digital data capture.
body_text: Metalworking shops today are under pressure from every direction: demanding customers in aerospace, medical, and oil and gas; tighter tolerances; and the need to prove that every part meets spec. That’s driving more facilities to invest in statistical process control (SPC) and data management tools that go far beyond paper logs and ad-hoc spreadsheets. “Manufacturers today are really trying to improve efficiency, improve throughput and reduce scrap, and in order to do all those things, they need the data about what they’ve made,” says Hany Abdel-Motaleb, data management and MeasurLink® sales engineer at Mitutoyo. “Being able to store and retain electronic records of inspection data for long periods of time is required, especially when you’re dealing with high-risk industries such as aerospace, medical, and oil and gas.” Hany Abdel-Motaleb, Data Management and MeasurLink® Sales Engineer, Mitutoyo MeasurLink is Mitutoyo’s data management and SPC software that’s designed to help shops collect, store and analyze inspection data over the long term. “Being able to store and retain electronic records of inspection data for long periods of time is required, especially when you’re dealing with high-risk industries such as aerospace, medical, and oil and gas,” he says. MeasurLink’s Latest Update Was Built for Busy, Short-Staffed Shops Abdel-Motaleb says MeasurLink 11, the newest version of the software introduced in July 2026, was redesigned to make implementation, navigation and daily use easier, especially for facilities that don’t have a dedicated SPC or metrology expert. “The main idea with version 11 was ease of use, so that really drove all of the new developments,” he says. For manufacturers dealing with lean staffing and constant firefighting, these are some of the changes that are meant to reduce friction: • Faster reporting. A revamped report template lets shops standardize on a few professional formats, rather than reinventing every report. Turnkey options, such as nonconformance reports, let users generate key documents in a couple of clicks. • Simpler navigation. A new landing page and quick-action buttons make it clearer where to start, whether you’re creating a new part, launching a job or reviewing results. • On-screen, context-aware help. Users can see guidance alongside the task they’re working on, instead of stopping to search manuals. One of the most tangible changes for small and mid-size shops is the quick setup feature, which shortens the time from “new part” to “collecting data.” “With quick setup, you can put all the information you want in it, and then hit finish, and now you can collect some data. So there’s no navigation needed. Simplicity is really what we were going for here,” Abdel-Motaleb says. Another operator-friendly touch is the dark mode option, which is aimed at reducing eye strain in dimly lit shop environments. From Prints to Plans in Minutes One of the most useful enhancements of MeasurLink is OCR (optical character recognition) and ballooning, which automates the process of turning engineering drawings into usable inspection plans by placing numbered circles (balloons) next to each dimension or design feature on an engineering blueprint. On a simple print, labeling dimensions by hand isn’t too difficult. But on real-world jobs, Abdel-Motaleb notes, it can quickly become overwhelming. “When we talk about things that aren’t a demo print, there may be 50, 100, 500 different characteristics that need to get labeled, and so to do that manually is very time-consuming and very tedious,” he says. With OCR and ballooning, MeasurLink automatically reads the dimensions, adds balloons to the print and builds an inspection plan directly from the drawing. That’s especially important for job shops that are running high-mix, low-volume work, where engineers might otherwise spend hours creating new plans for each job. Instead of manually rebuilding inspection plans as often as 20 times a day, shops can move from print to inspection much faster, while still capturing the structured data they need for SPC and quality documentation. Turning Data Into Action on the Shop Floor From a management perspective, the value of SPC shows up when it changes what happens on the floor in real time by catching issues before they become expensive scrap or customer complaints. On the operator side, MeasurLink presents results as they’re collected. When a measurement falls outside the tolerance band, the software forces a pause. “When you capture some data and it’s in the red, the operator knows that it’s out of specification and that stops everything, and they can document the reasons,” Abdel-Motaleb says. Capturing a simple reason code at that moment—such as tool breakage, setup error or wrong offset—gives engineers and supervisors a much clearer picture of where problems are coming from. Just as important is what happens before the data goes out of spec. Rather than waiting until parts fail, the software can watch for trends that suggest trouble may be brewing ahead. “When the data shows several points starting to trend downward, that’s the time to act,” he adds. “MeasurLink can detect those trends, alert the operator, and prompt corrective action so you fix the issue before it turns into scrap.” A common example is tool wear: As a cutting tool approaches the end of its life, dimensions can start drifting. By linking those trends to specific tools or machines, shops can fine-tune tool-change intervals and avoid both premature changes and late, scrap-generating ones. Digital, Push-Button Data Capture Operators Will Actually Use For many manufacturing facilities, the hardest part of implementing SPC is getting consistent, reliable data from busy operators. If data entry is slow or painful, people will revert to shortcuts. That’s why MeasurLink’s emphasis on digital, push-button data capture matters. The goal is to connect directly to gages and systems so that recording results is as simple as pressing a button. “The idea is to do this electronically and automatically, essentially at the push of a button,” Abdel-Motaleb says. “You want to make it easy for machinists, operators and inspectors by giving them digital tools where they don’t have to stop what they’re doing to type data in.” Video : TOOLING UP: How to Simplify Digital Data Collection

title: Loneliness in England: New Study Highlights a Growing Public Health Challenge
summary: A major study of more than 135,000 people across England has highlighted the widespread nature of loneliness and social isolation, with researchers warning that the issue should be treated as a public health concern affecting people across all stages of adulthood. body_text: A major study of more than 135,000 people across England has highlighted the widespread nature of loneliness and social isolation, with researchers warning that the issue should be treated as a public health concern affecting people across all stages of adulthood. The study, led by researchers at Imperial College London, found that almost one in six participants reported feeling lonely often or always. More than one in five also said they frequently experienced a lack of companionship, felt left out, or felt isolated. The research provides one of the most detailed examinations to date of loneliness, social connection, neighbourhood trust and social capital across England. It also suggests that the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic may still be influencing people's experiences of loneliness and isolation several years after the pandemic began. COVID-19 Pandemic Linked to Lasting Feelings of Isolation The researchers found that 43.8% of participants said the COVID-19 pandemic had increased their feelings of loneliness. Almost half, 48.2%, reported that the pandemic had increased their feelings of isolation. These findings are significant because social restrictions during the pandemic changed how people interacted with family, friends, colleagues and their wider communities. Although many restrictions have ended, the study suggests that their effects may have persisted for a substantial proportion of people. Professor Azeem Majeed, from Imperial College London's School of Public Health and senior author of the research, said loneliness can affect both mental and physical health and is something he encounters in primary care. He also emphasised that loneliness should not be viewed simply as an issue affecting older people. Instead, it can affect people throughout adulthood and may require responses that involve healthcare services as well as communities and local organisations. Loneliness Is Not Limited to Older People Loneliness is sometimes associated primarily with older adults, but the INTERACT study presents a broader picture. The researchers surveyed people aged 16 and over, and participants came from different age groups and backgrounds. The largest group represented in the study was people aged over 65, who accounted for 32.4% of respondents. People aged 56 to 65 made up another 24.5%, while 16.2% were aged 46 to 55. Younger adults were also represented, with 6.2% of respondents aged 16 to 25 and 9.6% aged 26 to 35. The findings therefore support the view that loneliness is a life-course issue rather than a problem confined to one particular age group. For some people, loneliness may result from major life changes, including moving to a new area, starting or leaving employment, relationship breakdown, retirement or bereavement. Others may experience loneliness despite having regular contact with other people. This distinction is important because loneliness is ultimately about a person's perceived quality of social connection, rather than simply the number of people around them. Cities Among Areas Where Loneliness Was Most Concentrated The study also examined the geographical distribution of loneliness across England. Researchers found clusters of higher reported loneliness in major urban areas, including London, Birmingham and Manchester. They suggest that these patterns may be consistent with the so-called "urban paradox", whereby large cities can offer extensive economic, cultural and social opportunities while some residents nevertheless experience lower levels of connection and wellbeing. Living in a densely populated area does not necessarily mean having strong social relationships. People can be surrounded by thousands of others and still feel disconnected from their local community. The researchers therefore argue that efforts to tackle loneliness need to consider the environments in which people live. Access to community facilities, social groups, public spaces and local services may all influence opportunities for people to form and maintain meaningful connections. Why Social Capital Matters Another important element of the INTERACT research is its focus on neighbourhood trust and social capital. Social capital broadly refers to the relationships, networks and shared norms that help people interact and support one another within a community. Strong social connections can create opportunities for people to participate in community life and access practical or emotional support. Dr Austen El-Osta, from Imperial College London's School of Public Health and the study's lead researcher, said the findings demonstrate that loneliness should not be regarded solely as a private experience. Instead, the research suggests that people's surroundings, social networks and local environments can all play a role. This means that addressing loneliness may require more than encouraging individuals to become more socially active. Communities may also need accessible spaces, activities and services that make it easier for people to participate and develop relationships. Important Limitations of the Research Despite the size of the study, the researchers caution against interpreting the results as an exact estimate of loneliness across the entire population of England. A total of 135,725 volunteers completed an online survey during a five-month period in 2023. Because participation was voluntary, people who were particularly interested in loneliness or affected by it may have been more likely to take part. The researchers also noted that the sample included a relatively high proportion of highly educated people and under-represented some minority ethnic groups. These factors mean the results should be understood as a detailed snapshot of experiences reported by study participants rather than a precise measurement of loneliness among every adult in England. Nevertheless, the scale of the dataset gives researchers an opportunity to investigate patterns that may otherwise be difficult to identify. It could also provide a useful benchmark for future research. Loneliness as a Public Health Issue The World Health Organization recognised loneliness as a global public health issue in 2023, reflecting growing evidence that social connection can have important implications for health and wellbeing. The INTERACT findings add to this wider body of research by examining loneliness alongside factors such as neighbourhood trust, social capital and geography. The researchers argue that healthcare providers, local authorities, community organisations and policymakers may all have a role in addressing the issue. A public health response could involve strengthening community infrastructure and making social opportunities easier to access. Local initiatives, volunteering, community groups and accessible public spaces may all provide opportunities for people to establish meaningful connections. Healthcare professionals can also play a role by recognising loneliness when it forms part of a person's wider health and wellbeing concerns. What Can Be Done About Loneliness? There is no single solution to loneliness because its causes and experiences differ from person to person. For some people, joining a community group or taking part in a regular activity may help create new social connections. Volunteering can provide another route into community life, while maintaining regular contact with family and friends can be valuable for people who are at risk of becoming isolated. At a wider level, communities can consider whether people have accessible places to meet, participate and build relationships. The key message from the INTERACT study is that loneliness should not automatically be treated as an individual failure to maintain relationships. The social and physical environment can influence people's opportunities to connect with others. Conclusion The INTERACT study offers a substantial new look at loneliness and social isolation in England. Almost one in six participants reported feeling lonely often or always, while many others reported lacking companionship or experiencing feelings of isolation. The research also highlights the continuing association between the COVID-19 pandemic and increased loneliness and isolation, as well as geographical patterns in major urban centres. While the study has important limitations and cannot be used to calculate the precise prevalence of loneliness across England, its findings underline the importance of understanding social connection as part of public health. Loneliness can affect people at different stages of life, and tackling it may require action that extends beyond healthcare. Stronger communities, accessible services and opportunities for meaningful participation could all contribute to a more connected society. Sources El-Osta, A., Alaa, A., Al-Ammouri, M., Altalib, S., Tristán-López, A. and Majeed, A. "Measuring loneliness at a national scale: The measuring loneliness in England (INTERACT) study's approach and initial findings." BMC Global and Public Health , 2026. DOI: 10.1186/s44263-026-00296-5. Imperial College London, study report on the INTERACT loneliness research, 13 August 2026. World Health Organization, information on social connection and loneliness as a global public health issue. NHS, information and support relating to loneliness. National Institute for Health and Care Research, Be Part of Research. Disclaimer This article is for general informational purposes only and is based on published research and publicly available information. It is not intended to provide medical or mental health advice, diagnosis or treatment. Anyone experiencing persistent loneliness, distress or concerns about their mental or physical health should consider speaking with an appropriate healthcare professional or support organisation.

title: Best Heist Movies of All Time You Need to Watch
summary: Looking for the best heist movies of all time? Here are the top picks that will keep you on the edge of your seat from start to finish.
body_text: Inspiration There is something absolutely electric about a well-planned heist. The tension, the clever twists, the moment everything either comes together perfectly or falls spectacularly apart. If you have ever found yourself staying up way too late just to find out whether the crew pulls it off, you are not alone. Heist movies have a way of making you root for the “bad guys” without even thinking twice about it. Whether you are a longtime fan of the genre or just getting into it, this list of the best heist movies of all time will give you plenty to binge. Grab your popcorn, because things are about to get interesting. And hey, if you enjoy stories about moving money across borders in clever ways, you might also enjoy reading about the best bank robbery movies and series to watch now . List of Content Toggle What Makes a Great Heist Movie? Before we dive into the list, it helps to understand what separates a truly great heist film from just another action flick. The best ones share a handful of things in common. 1. A Plan Worth Following The setup matters just as much as the payoff. Great heist movies spend serious time showing you the plan, the team, and the obstacles. You need to understand what is at stake before you can feel the rush when things go sideways. 2. Characters You Actually Care About You do not root for a heist crew because of the money. You root for them because of who they are. The best films in this genre give every character a reason to be there and a reason for you to care whether they make it out. 3. Unexpected Twists A predictable heist is a boring heist. The movies that stick with you are the ones where you think you have figured everything out, and then the rug gets pulled right from under you. The Best Heist Movies of All Time Here is the real reason you are here. These are the films that defined the genre, influenced countless others, and are still wildly entertaining no matter how many times you watch them. 1. Ocean’s Eleven (2001) If you have never seen Ocean’s Eleven , stop everything and fix that immediately. Steven Soderbergh’s remake is slick, stylish, and endlessly rewatchable. George Clooney, Brad Pitt, and an all-star ensemble plan an almost impossible triple-casino robbery in Las Vegas. The banter alone is worth the watch. 2. Heat (1995) Heat is widely considered one of the greatest crime films ever made, and for good reason. Al Pacino and Robert De Niro on opposite sides of the law, circling each other in Los Angeles. It is long, yes, but every single minute earns its place. The bank heist sequence is legendary. 3. The Italian Job (2003) Mini Coopers weaving through the streets of Los Angeles carrying stolen gold. What more do you need? The Italian Job is a fun, fast-moving heist film that never takes itself too seriously, and it works brilliantly because of that. 4. Inside Man (2006) Spike Lee’s Inside Man is a masterclass in misdirection. Clive Owen plays a bank robber who seems to have no obvious exit strategy, and Denzel Washington is the detective trying to figure out what is really going on. The ending will have you rewinding to catch everything you missed. 5. Rififi (1955) This French classic set the blueprint for nearly every heist movie that came after it. The nearly thirty-minute silent safecracking sequence is still one of the most tension-filled scenes in cinema history. If you appreciate where the genre came from, Rififi is essential viewing. 6. The Town () Ben Affleck directs and stars in this gritty Boston-set thriller about a career bank robber trying to get out of the game. The Town blends genuine emotional weight with some of the best action sequences in modern heist cinema. 7. Now You See Me () Four magicians use their performances as cover for elaborate heists, staying one step ahead of the FBI the entire time. Now You See Me is pure entertainment, and the twist at the end genuinely earns its place among the genre’s best moments. 8. Baby Driver () Edgar Wright’s Baby Driver is unlike anything else on this list. It follows a young getaway driver whose life is set entirely to music, and the film uses that concept to create chase sequences that are borderline hypnotic. The soundtrack is half the experience. 9. Inception () Yes, Inception is a heist movie. Instead of stealing money, Dom Cobb’s team steals ideas from inside people’s dreams. Christopher Nolan takes the genre to a completely different level, and the result is one of the most ambitious films ever made. 10. Logan Lucky () Steven Soderbergh returns with a brilliantly offbeat heist set during a NASCAR race in North Carolina. Logan Lucky is funny, surprisingly clever, and has one of the most satisfying endings in recent memory. Daniel Craig playing a bleach-blond safecracker named Joe Bang is reason enough to watch. Hidden Gems Worth Adding to Your Watchlist Beyond the big names, there are a handful of underrated heist films that deserve far more attention than they usually get. 1. Thief (1981) Michael Mann’s debut feature is a moody, atmospheric portrait of a professional safecracker trying to build a normal life. James Caan is magnetic in the lead role, and the film’s electronic score by Tangerine Dream is unforgettable. 2. The Killing (1956) Stanley Kubrick directing a racetrack heist with a non-linear structure that was years ahead of its time. The Killing is compact, precise, and genuinely thrilling. It also clearly influenced Tarantino’s early work. 3. A Fish Called Wanda (1988) If you want your heist movie with a healthy dose of absurd British comedy, this is the one. It won an Academy Award for John Cleese’s screenplay and remains one of the funniest crime films ever made. Tips for Building the Perfect Heist Movie Night Got a group of friends coming over? Here is how to make the most of a heist movie marathon. Start with a lighter film like Ocean’s Eleven or The Italian Job to set a fun tone. Go deeper mid-session with something meatier like Heat or Inception . End with a twist-heavy film like Inside Man so you finish on a conversation-starting note. Mix eras to appreciate how the genre has evolved over the decades. Have snacks ready because pausing at the wrong moment in a heist movie is practically a crime in itself. See Also: Best Bank Robbery Movies and Series to Watch Now, Including Netflix Hits The best heist movies of all time share one thing in common: they make you feel like you are in on the plan. Whether you are a fan of slick Hollywood blockbusters or classic black-and-white tension, this genre has something for everyone. Pick one from the list, settle in, and enjoy the ride. title: Baltimore County Police Department orders second H125 through Davenport Aviation
summary: The aircraft represents the department’s second new H125 acquisition through Davenport.
body_text: Davenport Aviation has announced the Baltimore County Police Department has placed an order for a new Airbus H125 helicopter. Purchased through Davenport Aviation’s GSA contract, the aircraft represents the department’s second new H125 acquisition through Davenport and will replace an older AS350B3 currently in service. The Baltimore County Police Department operates a fleet of three Airbus helicopters supporting public safety missions across the county. Following delivery of the new aircraft, the department will maintain its three-helicopter fleet, with two of the three aircraft modernized to the H125 platform. The department’s Aviation Unit supports a wide range of missions across Baltimore County, including routine patrol, search and rescue, command and control, and emergency response. The replacement of the AS350B3 reflects the department’s continued investment in modernizing its aviation capabilities while maintaining the fleet size required to support daily operations. The new H125 will provide updated technology, proven performance, and mission flexibility for demanding airborne law enforcement and public safety missions. “We’re honored that the Baltimore County Police Department has once again chosen Davenport Aviation to support the modernization of its aviation fleet,” said Chris Arnold, Director of Government Sales at Davenport Aviation. “The H125 has proven itself as an exceptional platform for airborne law enforcement, and we’re proud to help deliver another aircraft that will serve the department and the citizens of Baltimore County for years to come.” The H125 is a versatile single-engine helicopter widely used by public safety agencies for patrol, search-and-rescue, surveillance, tactical support, and other specialized missions. Its performance, maneuverability, advanced avionics, and mission flexibility make it well suited for the Baltimore County Police Department’s diverse operational requirements. Mission equipment integration and aircraft completion will be performed by Metro Aviation in Shreveport, Louisiana. The completed aircraft is anticipated to be delivered to the Baltimore County Police Department in October of 2027. The purchase is being completed through Davenport Aviation’s GSA contract, providing Baltimore County with a streamlined procurement path for the aircraft and associated program support. The department’s first new H125 was also purchased through Davenport’s GSA contract, continuing an established relationship between the two organizations. Davenport Aviation is proud to continue supporting the Baltimore County Police Department and looks forward to working alongside Metro Aviation throughout the completion and delivery process. This press release was prepared and distributed by Davenport Aviation.

title: Kartoon Studios to Participate in the Lytham Partners 2026 Consumer & Technology Investor Summit on August 18, 2026
body_text: Kartoon Studios to Participate in the Lytham Partners 2026 Consumer & Technology Investor Summit on August 18, 2026 Download as PDF August 18, 2026 BEVERLY HILLS, CA / ACCESS Newswire / August 18, 2026 / Kartoon Studios, Inc. (NYSE American:TOON) ("Kartoon Studios" or the "Company"), a global entertainment company creating, producing, distributing and licensing children's and family content, today announced that it will participate in a webcast presentation at the Lytham Partners 2026 Consumer & Technology Investor Summit, taking place virtually on Tuesday, August 18, 2026. The webcast will take place at 12:30 p.m. ET on Tuesday, August 18, 2026. The webcast can be accessed by visiting the summit home page at https://lythampartners.com/cts2026/ or directly at https://lythampartners.com/cts2026/toon . A replay will also be available through the same links. During the discussion, management is expected to provided investors with an overview of Kartoon Studios' ongoing transformation and addresses several key topics, including: The Company's strategic shift from primarily providing production and creative services for third parties toward developing and commercializing intellectual property that Kartoon Studios owns or controls, should enable the Company to participate in multiple revenue streams and retain more of the long-term franchise economics. The Company's priorities over the next 12 to 24 months, including bringing Hundred Acre Wood - Kartoon Studios' original reimagining inspired by A.A. Milne's classic stories - to market across content, distribution, licensing, publishing and consumer products. The continued development of the Stan Lee Universe, beginning with Stan Lee's Superhero Pets , and the opportunity to monetize original properties across animation, publishing, digital media, licensing and consumer products. The Company's strengthened financial position, including more than $40 million in cash and marketable securities and no long-term debt as of June 30, 2026, as well as management's disciplined approach to liquidity, capital allocation and investment in core intellectual property. The Company's efforts to simplify its portfolio and cost structure, including the recent sale of the Frederator Channel Network business while retaining key Frederator Studios intellectual property for future distribution and licensing opportunities, as well as the principal execution milestones investors should monitor going forward. Kartoon Studios has retained Lytham Partners to lead a strategic investor relations and shareholder communications program designed to broaden the Company's dialogue with institutional investors and analysts, strengthen investor understanding of its evolving business model and provide more consistent communication around the Company's strategy, execution milestones and long-term shareholder value creation initiatives. About Kartoon Studios Kartoon Studios (NYSE American:TOON) is a global, vertically integrated children's and family entertainment company turning owned and controlled intellectual property into enduring, multi-platform franchises. The Company develops, produces, distributes, licenses and monetizes content across the full value chain, creating multiple revenue opportunities and long-term brand value. Kartoon Studios' growth portfolio includes Hundred Acre Wood and the Stan Lee Universe, alongside established brands and an extensive programming library. The Company operates Mainframe Studios and Toon Media Networks, as well as Beacon Media Group, a full-service marketing, communications, and media agency subsidiary of Kartoon Studios focused on children and family. title: Innovating with AI Because Reinvention Is in Cirque du Soleil’s DNA
summary: Cirque du Soleil knows firsthand how to leverage SAP technology not only to run its operations, but also to reinvent them.
body_text: For audiences, Cirque du Soleil is about wonder: gravity-defying performers, breathtaking costumes, immersive music, and moments that feel almost impossible. But behind every performance is something just as remarkable: a highly complex global business operation. It reinvented circus arts and became a world leader in live entertainment, performing for more than 365 million spectators in 90 countries. Today, the organization operates 38 shows in cities around the world, supported by over 4,000 touring artists and staff from more than 80 countries. Each touring show functions like a moving profit center. A production may operate in Mexico City, then move to London, then Paris—bringing with it new companies, employees, assets, tax requirements, local regulations, merchandising operations, and artists from dozens of nationalities. As Philippe Lalumière, vice president of Information Technology at Cirque du Soleil, explains, “People underestimate the complexity of running a circus.” An enterprise AI platform built for your business Explore SAP Business AI Platform Orchestrating an autonomous accounts payable process This is especially true for the company’s accounts payable (AP) department. Every year, more than 70,000 invoices flow through Cirque du Soleil, non-stop, 24/7. Around 40% of vendor inquiries are standard requests for invoice status. But answering those questions was far from simple. AP specialists had to search across systems, review invoice histories, understand payment status, determine the cause of delays, and manually respond. The work was repetitive, time-consuming, and emotionally draining. “From a morale point of view, receiving e-mails from suppliers, some of them a bit impolite because they’re asking, ‘When are we going to get paid?’—it’s not a fun job,” Lalumière says. Finding the right problem to solve—putting AI into action As an SAP customer for more than 25 years, Cirque du Soleil knows firsthand how to leverage SAP technology not only to run its operations, but also to reinvent them. Cirque du Soleil, known as an early adopter and leader in digital transformation, was approached by SAP AppHaus with a question: how could SAP generative AI technology be used to improve your business processes? The answer emerged through collaborative workshops involving SAP, Cirque du Soleil’s IT team, and business users across its departments. Accounts payable quickly rose to the top due to its lean structure, high volume of interactions, and clear automation potential. And the choice aligned with the broader business evolution—AP automation is one of the most widely adopted AI use cases across industries. With a clear opportunity identified, Cirque du Soleil and SAP moved from ideation to execution, developing an AI-powered solution that automated AP processes and improved responsiveness. AI enters stage right—from vision to reality The workshops led to something more than an automation project—they led to Genato, a multilingual AI agent that now works alongside the AP team. The polyglot agent scans the AP inbox, analyzes sentiment, identifies urgency, extracts invoice numbers from messages and attachments, connects to SAP data to retrieve invoice status, and drafts a response for human review. If it cannot find an invoice or resolve an inquiry, it flags the issue. “Trust in the quality of the answers coming from the agent was an initial concern,” Lalumière says. “But, the team quickly realized that Genato’s information was spot on.” Together, Genato and the AP team now serve Cirque du Soleil’s diverse global supplier network more efficiently. Lalumière, however, is clear about one thing: “Yes, AI is a very powerful tool, but it’s not pixie dust. Sprinkling AI into processes is not going to solve everything. There is work involved.” That work included designing appropriate connectors and integrating with the company’s SAP and AP systems using SAP Business AI Platform . This enterprise AI foundation can bring together capabilities and technologies (think SAP Business Data Cloud, Business Transformation Management solutions, and SAP Business AI), unifying AI, data, process context, and governance, so customers can build, integrate, scale, and run AI that delivers business impact while working to ensure the solution is sustainable and cost-efficient. The impact was evident almost immediately. Generative AI began prioritizing urgent supplier requests, retrieving invoice information, drafting responses, and translating communications automatically, delivering measurable improvements across the AP organization: 97.92% improvement in handling priority requests 25% reduction in AP backlog 25% faster response times for non-urgent inquiries Improved vendor satisfaction and employee morale The impact on employees cannot be overstated. By removing repetitive research and emotionally charged supplier follow-up from the team’s workload, Genato has become more than a tool. “We now include Genato as a virtual team member,” Lalumière explains, “It’s a paradigm shift.” That adoption is the clearest sign of success. Lalumière recalls that after the prototype moved into production, one of the end users made her feelings clear: “No, no, no, you cannot take it away from me! There is no way I’m going to live without it now.” Today, she is one of the solution’s biggest ambassadors. Collectively, the solution demonstrates how AI can be introduced into a focused business process, quickly earn user trust, and create a blueprint for broader enterprise innovation. As Lalumière puts it, “You could say we’re an SAP shop.” The next act of AI innovation For Cirque du Soleil, accounts payable is only the beginning. Lalumière believes that “AI is a huge and beautiful tool, but you still need human judgment to prioritize use cases and move forward.” He also sees AI evolving across three layers: personal productivity with solutions such as Joule; AI applied to business processes, such as Genato; and, eventually, AI embedded in the audience experience itself. “I think we’re at the dawn of a new era of circus arts,” he says. His advice to others beginning their AI journey is simple: start small, involve users early, and be willing to experiment. “Try a small proof of concept and be ready to throw them away,” Lalumière says. “The AI train is moving, and you have to hop on.” For a company built on reinvention, transforming accounts payable may seem far removed from the spotlight, but for Lalumière, the principle is the same: innovation happens when people are willing to rethink what’s possible. Today, that mindset is improving back-office operations. Tomorrow, it may help redefine the audience’s experience. The full episode Learn more about how Cirque du Soleil has transformed its AP process using AI to improve vendor relations, staff morale, and overall department productivity: Thought leadership podcast : Lalumière sat down with Thulium CEO Tamara McCleary to discuss the shifts in the business and in the world that inspired Cirque du Soleil’s AI vision and application, and how others can learn from their journey. Practitioners’ video : Lalumière shares technical insights and advice with Timo Elliott, VP and global innovation evangelist at SAP, about Cirque du Soleil’s AI applications, user experiences, and how the combination of both is essential to Cirque du Soleil’s automation journey. Explore the on-demand series. Sid Misra is CMO of SAP Business AI Platform Technology Foundation. Top image courtesy of Cirque du Soleil.
